messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are an expert space systems engineer for Project Dyson, a non-profit
planning the construction of a Dyson swarm.

Provide a DETAILED technical proposal for: **Organizational Infrastructure**
Context: Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure (0A)
Accepted scope: Legal, governance and coordination infrastructure, with a full specification (round 2 found none).

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- resize · bom-0-7 organization · supported by all · quantity: 1 · cost: Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M; GPT $150–350M · confidence: medium (GPT)

Critical technologies (TRL re-baseline, panel envelope):
- T26 Deep-space communications and resilient command service: TRL 3 now, target 6, AD² 4, architecture-change

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

### Round-2 reconciliation for this item

# Reconciliation: bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure (Phase 0, Round 2)

**Panel:** Claude Opus 5.5 ("Claude"), Gemini 3.8 Flash ("Gemini"), GPT-6.1 Sol ("GPT").

**Rapporteur's role:** This document consolidates and attributes the panel's positions. It does not decide between them. Arithmetic was re-checked where models showed working. Discrepancies found are reported in the text and in the Reviewer note; they are not corrected silently.

---

## 1. Verdict matrix

| Finding | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0-F13**: Organizational infrastructure has no specification | agree | agree | agree |
| **P0-F15**: Eight of nine concluded deliberations not written back | partly | agree | partly |

**P0-F13.** The panel agrees unanimously that the gap is real. The models differ on how to label its severity:

- **Claude** proposes a split label: "major (schedule) / minor (cost)."
- **Gemini** calls it a "major blocker."
- **GPT** rates it "major for the hardware-development phase; minor only for a discussion community."

**P0-F15.** All three agree that rq-0-29 has not been written back into bom-0-7.

- **Claude and GPT** say they cannot verify the repository-wide "eight of nine" count. Both say write-back must be adapted or dispositioned, not copied verbatim.
- **Gemini** accepts the count and proposes adding compliance lines directly.

---

## 2. Agreed changes

These are specification changes that all three models support, explicitly or by direct equivalent.

| Change | Consolidated value / range | Support and notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Legal architecture** | **2 entities (range 2–3)**: a governance association (Swiss Verein) plus a separately accountable operating / licence-holding entity | All three. Claude names Luxembourg or the US as lead candidates. Gemini names a Luxembourg S.A. or a US C-Corp/PBC. GPT treats Swiss as provisional and would choose the operator jurisdiction only after a comparison. |
| **Orbital allocation for bom-0-7** | **0 t/yr mass, 0 MW orbital power, 0 t/yr propellant** | All three, high confidence. |
| **Terrestrial power** | **0.01–0.05 MW**, not drawn from bom-0-5 | Claude (interface), Gemini (0.02 MW, range 0.01–0.05), GPT (0.01–0.05 MW). |
| **PM/SE/MA excluded from bom-0-7** | Exclusion | All three. Claude: placing it here "would mix governance with execution." Gemini: it "breaks standard aerospace WBS." GPT: it is separate scope with its own owner. |
| **Endowment / liquidity treated as financing, not expenditure** | Shown as a separate line | All three. Sizing differs; see §3. |
| **Functions added to bom-0-7 from other deliberations** | Resource-rights legal work (rq-0-14), independent safety authority (rq-0-18), independent cost-estimate review (rq-0-28) | All three. Claude sizes these at $3–10M one-time plus 1–2 FTE for resource rights, and 1–2 FTE each for the two review functions. GPT includes them within its staffing allowance. Gemini adds "explicit compliance, legal advisory, and assurance tracking lines." Claude flags that *where* independent review sits is still an open values question (§3). |
| **Use existing open licences, not a bespoke copyleft** | CERN OHL v2 for hardware; Creative Commons for documents | All three. Claude specifies OHL v2-S plus CC BY-SA 4.0 and a restricted export annex. Gemini specifies CERN OHL v2 / CC-BY-SA. GPT says to choose the OHL variant deliberately and use a separately controlled restricted annex. |
| **Archive replication** | **3 independent copies with regular restore testing** | Claude (3 replicas, annual restore test), Gemini ("triple-redundant… continuous restore testing"), GPT (3 independently administered copies, annual restore). Archive *volume* is not agreed; see §3. |
| **Staffing order of magnitude** | Approximately 15 FTE; the ranges all models share are **14–20 FTE** | Claude 18 (14–25), Gemini 15 (10–20), GPT 16 (12–20). The 14–20 overlap is the rapporteur's intersection of the three ranges, not a value any model proposed. |
| **Export classification before publication** | Required | Claude: classify "before publication, not after." GPT: a restricted annex is needed after export review. Gemini raises ITAR/EAR as an open question and as a disconfirmation test for its entity decision. |

The following points have **two-model agreement, with Gemini silent or not explicit**. They are not unanimous:

- Charter Trust becomes a Phase 0 design study only.
- Sortition is used for advisory or oversight panels only.
- Funding caps become disclosed targets with time-limited exceptions.
- Leadership overlap is 3–12 months.
- The initial liquidity target is 1–2 years of opex.
- Phase 0 has an uncrewed baseline.
- A disposition register is kept for every deliberation.
- Programme-scale governance or acceptance gates replace or supplement the 100-contributor / $50K triggers.

Supporting physics checks (Claude and GPT both re-derived these; Gemini did not address them):

- **Rotation for gravity zones:** 1.5–2.6 rpm for 0.05–0.15 g at r = 20 m.
- **Boil-off at 1 kW heat leak:** about 194 kg/day LH₂ or 406 kg/day LOX.
- **Meaning of "25 kt/yr":** if it means hydrogen output, electrolysis alone exceeds the 100 MW phase supply.
  - Claude: 140–190 MW.
  - GPT: 143–171 MW calendar-average.

Both refer this ambiguity to a phase power closure, not to bom-0-7.

---

## 3. Preserved divergences

### 3.1 bom-0-7 cost (10-year equivalent)

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **$110M, range $55–200M** (including 20% contingency). Primary form is a run-rate of $9M/yr ($4.4–16.3M) plus $5M one-time ($2–8M). 5-year equivalent: $55M ($29–108M). | Claude | A run-rate removes the 5-year vs 10-year confusion that blocked round 1. Inputs: 14–25 FTE at $200–350k; outside counsel $1–4M/yr; filings $0.1–0.5M/yr; insurance $0.3–2M/yr; IT/archive $0.2–1M/yr. Confidence low. |
| **$120M, range $80–190M**, on a 10-year baseline | Gemini | Bottom-up build: setup $5M; 12–18 FTE at $275k ($40M); external counsel and filings $15M; in-orbit TPL premiums $30M; archive $10M; 20% contingency $20M. Confidence medium. |
| **$65M, range $40–105M** (25% uncertainty allowance; constant 2026 USD) | GPT | Formula C = 1.25[formation + T(N·c + services)], with 12–20 FTE at $180–260k and services of $0.8–2.8M/yr. The ranges are scenario bounds, not a confidence interval. 5-year equivalent: $20–55M. GPT concludes that "$50M could be workable for a narrower five-year scope." Confidence low. |

**Main drivers of the spread:**

- **Inclusion of TPL premiums.** Gemini includes $30M; Claude about $3–20M; GPT excludes premiums.
- **Burdened FTE rate.** The models' rates span $180k to $350k.
- **Contingency.** 20% (Claude, Gemini) versus 25% (GPT).

**Arithmetic checks:**

- Claude's and GPT's working reproduces.
- Gemini's component sum ($120M) reproduces.
- Gemini's staffing figure is internally inconsistent: the text says 12–18 FTE, the parameter table says 10–20.

### 3.2 Costing duration

- **Gemini:** 10 years (range 7–12), high confidence.
- **GPT:** 10 years (sensitivity 5–10), low confidence, "subject to phase approval."
- **Claude:** declines to fix a duration. It states a run-rate and shows both 5-year and 10-year totals.

Claude and GPT both list the 0A/0B phase boundary as an open question.

### 3.3 Severity label for P0-F13

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Split label: major (schedule) / minor (cost) | Claude | Cost is 0.3–1.3% of the phase. On schedule, authorization, ITU and planetary-protection work gate every flight item. Under a cost-of-delay (CD3) argument, delay costs about $80–160M per year against a function costing $4–16M per year. The label would be falsified if first launch is scheduled more than 7 years out. |
| Major blocker | Gemini | Hardware procurement "cannot legally execute" without an authorized operating entity. |
| Stage-dependent: major for the hardware phase, minor for a discussion community | GPT | The 0.32% ratio "neither proves inadequacy nor validates adequacy." The real defects are missing scope, duration and allocation. |

### 3.4 Third-party liability (TPL) and insurance placement

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| In-orbit TPL premiums inside bom-0-7 at **$3–20M over 10 years** (point estimate $8M); retained risk as a separate financing line | Claude | Launch TPL sits under the launch provider's licence. Liability Convention Art. III applies a fault standard in space. Deep-space operations at about 1 AU have "essentially no third parties." Claude judges round-1 figures ($15–120M; $75M reserve) too high. The estimate is reopened if bom-0-4 brings material toward Earth. No broker quote. |
| In-orbit TPL premiums inside bom-0-7 at **$30M (range $15–60M)**; launch MPL wrapped into launch contracts | Gemini | Market capacity is $50–250M of coverage; premiums are estimated for fleet deployment over 10 years. |
| **Only insurance administration** sits in bom-0-7; flight premiums and loss reserves are excluded | GPT | Statutory liability amounts, maximum probable loss, policy limit, premium and funded reserve are distinct quantities. Launch-provider coverage "does not automatically remove all customer exposures." No credible number follows without quotes. |

### 3.5 Archive volume and cost

- **Claude:** governance ingest of 1 TB/yr (0.5–5). Mirrors 10–100 TB/yr of engineering data, which is owned by PM/SE. Storage costs about $72k/yr; labour and testing dominate.
- **Gemini:** 50 TB cumulative over 10 years (20–200), costed at $10M ($5–15M). Also lists a 5–10 TB/yr ground-segment data interface.
- **GPT:** 2–20 TB/yr logical ingest, giving 60–600 TB over 10 years with 3 copies. Excludes raw telemetry. Averages 0.5–5 Mbit/s.

Claude and GPT both reject the round-1 10 Gbit/s backbone. Gemini does not repeat that proposal this round.

### 3.6 Board and Charter Trust parameters

- **Board size:**
  - Claude: 7 (5–9), staggered 3–4-year terms, 8-year service limit.
  - GPT: 5–7, staggered 3-year terms, normally two consecutive terms.
  - Gemini: gives a staggered term of 4 years (3–5), labelled "literature / high confidence." It does not state a board size.
- **Charter Trust:**
  - Claude and GPT: a design study only in Phase 0, established later at a milestone.
  - Gemini: has Entity A maintain "sortition-based Charter Trust studies." However, its preferred Option 2 has the Verein that "sorts trustees." Gemini's open questions call the role, screening and term length (4 vs 15 years) "disputed." Its position on establishing the Trust in Phase 0 is therefore not explicit.
- **Sortition evidence:**
  - Claude and GPT rate it low. The evidence comes from deliberative mini-publics and citizens' assemblies, not asset-holding trusts.
  - Gemini sees risks of "paralysis or capture by permanent staff" and leaves the question open.

### 3.7 Operating-entity jurisdiction

- **Claude:** leans toward Luxembourg (or Japan) because it has a mission-authorization regime for resource activities. The US has resource rights but "an unsettled path" for novel activities. Legal opinion decides.
- **Gemini:** scores the "Luxembourg S.A. / US Corp" bifurcated option highest. It does not choose between the two.
- **GPT:** select only after comparing authorization, liability, tax, funding and export control. High confidence that a selection is needed; low confidence on which state wins.

### 3.8 Swiss space-law status (factual divergence)

- **Claude:** Switzerland has no comprehensive space act in force; a draft is in progress (*verify*).
- **Gemini:** Switzerland "lacks domestic implementing legislation for private off-world resource exploitation." Gemini states this with high confidence.
- **GPT:** "Swiss legal status should not be asserted from stale text"; verify at entity selection.

### 3.9 Crew and 14 CFR Part 460

- **Claude:** the baseline states no crew carriage is authorized in Phase 0. A Part 460 path applies only if crew are ever carried.
- **GPT:** uncrewed baseline. Part 460 "is not a general deep-space human-rating standard." Structural reinforcement should not be called "human-rating."
- **Gemini:** bom-0-7 should "handle crew-flight liability (e.g. 14 CFR 460 / FAA AST)." It does not state an uncrewed baseline.

### 3.10 Planetary protection

- **Claude:** expects COSPAR Category I/II, assessed by a national agency and "not 'filed with COSPAR'."
- **Gemini:** lists "COSPAR Cat II clearance" and "COSPAR notifications" as filings.
- **GPT:** COSPAR policy is "not itself a universal permit." Spectral class alone is insufficient; a mission-specific determination is required.

### 3.11 Placement of independent safety and cost review

- **Claude:** these are values trade-offs.
  - Placing review in bom-0-7 gives independence.
  - Placing it in PM/SE gives integration and speed.
- **GPT:** include it in bom-0-7 staffing, but "distinguish organizational review from detailed engineering assurance."
- **Gemini:** place it in bom-0-7.

### 3.12 Phase split

Claude leans toward separating the volunteer research and governance stage into its own phase, noting that "reasonable people differ." GPT and Gemini raise the 0A/0B and duration boundary but do not take that position.

---

## 4. Proposed BOM delta

**These are proposals for human review. None are adopted.**

| # | Action | Item | Supporting models | Qty | Unit-cost range (USD) | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | **Resize** | bom-0-7 Organizational infrastructure (10-year equivalent) | All three; ranges differ | 1 | Claude $55–200M; Gemini $80–190M; GPT $40–105M | Claude low; Gemini medium; GPT low |
| D2 | **Split** | Organizational liquidity reserve, as financing not expenditure | Claude, GPT (in YAML). Gemini endorses financing treatment but does not size it. | 1 | Claude $9–30M (1–2 yr opex); GPT $3–16M | Claude medium; GPT low |
| D3 | **Add** | Programme management, systems engineering and mission assurance (PM/SE/MA) | Claude, Gemini (sized). GPT supports the account *or* confirming it is already in prime contracts, and withdraws dollar ranges. | 1 | Claude $1.5–3.5B (10–22% of hardware); Gemini $1.5–2.5B (point estimate $1.8B) | Claude low; Gemini not stated |
| D4 | **Add** | Launch and delivery to operating site | Claude, Gemini (sized). GPT says the scope is required but needs a mass budget first. | 1 | Claude $2–20B (0.9–3.7 kt to LEO); Gemini $1.5–4.0B (point estimate $2.5B; "~100+ tonnes") | Claude low; Gemini not stated |
| D5 | **Add** | Mission operations and ground segment | Claude, Gemini (sized). GPT says the scope is required, unsized. | 1 | Claude $0.5–1.5B; Gemini $0.4–1.0B (point estimate $0.6B) | Claude low; Gemini not stated |
| D6 | **Add** | Risk-retention / self-insurance reserve, as financing | Claude (unsized placeholder). GPT says separate with no number. Gemini raises the backstop as an open question. | 1 | Claude [0, 1.5B], "size only after broker indications" | Low / unsized |

**Notes on the deltas:**

- **Launch mass basis for D4.** Claude's estimate (0.9–3.7 kt, of which the arrays alone are 0.7–1 kt) and Gemini's ("~100+ tonnes") differ by roughly an order of magnitude. Neither is backed by a phase mass budget.
- **TPL premiums.** These are not a separate delta line. They sit inside D1 for Claude ($3–20M) and Gemini ($15–60M), and outside bom-0-7 for GPT; see §3.4.
- **Claude's projected phase total.** If D3–D5 are adopted, Claude projects the phase total at roughly $20–40B rather than $15.7B.
- **GPT's position on prior deltas.** GPT recommends that round-1 deltas B3–B6 be retained as scope decisions, but with their dollar ranges withdrawn.

---

## 5. Open questions and what would settle them

| Question | Raised by | What would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| Do bom-0-1 to bom-0-6 prices already include PM/SE, launch and operations? | All three | A WBS scope dictionary for each item. Claude names this as the falsifier for its cost hypotheses H1–H3 and for D3. GPT uses it as the falsifier for its scope assumption. |
| What is the phase mass budget? | Claude, GPT | A phase mass budget, which is a prerequisite for D4. Claude notes the arrays alone may be 0.7–1 kt. |
| Phase 0 duration and the 0A/0B boundary | All three | An approved phase schedule. For Claude, first launch more than 7 years out would falsify the "major (schedule)" label. |
| Which state authorizes the operator, and can a Verein control it without being treated as the de facto operator or carrying its torts? | All three | Counsel opinions in the candidate states (Claude, Gemini) and regulator engagement (Claude). |
| Does any trajectory bring material toward Earth or cislunar space? | Claude, GPT | The mission profile. Claude says this moves TPL by about 10× or more and changes the planetary-protection outcome. |
| Actual insurance premiums, limits, exclusions and retention needs | All three | Broker indications or quotes; launch contract terms; identity of the FAA licence holder of record (Claude). |
| What does "25 kt/yr" (rq-0-14) measure: water, hydrogen, combined propellant or delivered product? | Claude, GPT | A defined production rate, location and availability, followed by a phase power-allocation closure. |
| Which specifications are ITAR/EAR-controlled, and what restricted annex is needed? | All three | An export classification study before publication. |
| Does evidence support sortition and long terms for asset-holding trusts? | All three | Claude points to the rq-0-29 action-5 persistence study. GPT points to funding-control simulations or a red-team takeover exercise. |
| Are the round-2 legal citations correct (CSLCA, Luxembourg 2017, 51 USC §50915, Swiss draft act, ITAR/EAR categories)? | Claude and GPT flag "verify" | Counsel verification. No model verified them. |
| What do the full deliberation records and repository history show (the "eight of nine" count)? | Claude, GPT | Repository audit. |
| Does Phase 0 include any crewed mission? | GPT, Claude | A baseline decision. Claude and GPT both recommend uncrewed. |
| Will regulators license an entity whose charter mandates copyleft publication, or accept sortition-based oversight? | Gemini | A licence-application or pre-application consultation outcome. |

---

## 6. Decision-quality audit

### 6.1 Mapping of decisions across models

| Topic | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entity structure and jurisdiction | Decision C (QOC) | Decision 1 (weighted scoring / QOC / Kepner-Tregoe) | Decision A (QOC) |
| bom-0-7 cost and scope | Decision A (ACH) | Decision 2 (partial scaffold) | Decision B (GRADE EtD) |
| Severity of P0-F13 | Decision B (CD3) | — | — |
| Charter Trust, sortition, terms | Decision D (GRADE EtD) | — | Decision C (GRADE EtD, ACH) |
| Insurance and compliance | Decision E | — | Decision D (QOC, assurance case) |
| PM/SE and launch additions | Decision F | (within Decision 2) | (within Decision E and §4) |
| Write-back and disposition | — | — | Decision E (ACH) |
| Archive, succession, reserves | — | — | Decision F (QOC) |

### 6.2 Weakest link named, per decision

| Topic | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entity / jurisdiction | **Information**: no legal citation verified | **Information**: no precedent for a copyleft entity doing deep-space resource extraction | **Information**: mission jurisdiction and funding sources unknown |
| Cost / scope | **Frame**: round 1 debated numbers before fixing scope and duration | Not stated | **Frame** in the earlier reconciliation; **information** in GPT's own estimate |
| Severity | **Values**: nobody stated what "severity" measures | — | — |
| Trust / sortition | **Information**: evidence quality mislabelled (Gemini's "high, literature") | — | **Information** for the sortition claim; **values** for independence versus fundability |
| Insurance / compliance | **Reasoning**: round 1 treated launch, in-orbit and deep-space liability as one exposure | — | **Information**: targets, flight profiles and contractual allocations absent |
| PM/SE / launch | **Alternatives**: round 1 never considered that launch could exceed hardware cost | — | — |
| Write-back | — | — | **Commitment**: previous reconciliation assigns no approval authority or closure dates |
| Archive / succession | — | — | **Information** on actual records; **commitment** to recurring exercises |

Where models agree:

- On entity structure, all three name **information** as the weakest link.
- On cost and scope, Claude and GPT both name **frame** for round 1.

### 6.3 Scaffold steps found missing or unsupported

**Claude, on round 1:**

- Scope and duration were not fixed before estimating (frame).
- Severity was used without a definition (values).
- Gemini's "high, literature" certainty for sortition and long terms is unsupported and should be **low**.
- The liability exposures were conflated.
- Launch costs were never placed among the alternatives.
- B4 (Claude's round-1 $2–8B launch) is "untraceable."

**GPT, on round 1:**

- Different scopes were compared "as if they were alternative prices for the same product."
- The reserve proposals "lack the warrant connecting risk exposure to dollar value"; the $75M reserve cannot be derived from a $100M liability amount.
- There is an arithmetic error: 20 FTE × $400k × 10 years = **$80M, not $90M**.
- The previous reconciliation identifies omissions without assigning approval authority.

**GPT, on method generally:**

- Legal and safety conditions are "musts," not weighted criteria.
- "A simple weighted score cannot legalize an otherwise infeasible option."
- Its own weights are "illustrative," not measured utilities.
- Its likelihood words are engineering judgement, not measured probabilities; the cost range is "plausible, not 'likely at 90%'."

**Claude, on its own outputs:**

- It gives numeric likelihoods with separate confidence statements. For example, the 10-year cost exceeding $50M is "likely (≈70–85%), confidence medium."
- GPT's caveat about judgement-based likelihoods applies to these figures, but GPT did not target Claude specifically.

**Gemini, on its own outputs:**

- **Decision 1** has a full nine-step scaffold.
- **Decision 2** covers only frame and type plus a trade-off narrative. It has no:
  - criteria weights;
  - matrix;
  - certainty statement;

# bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure: Phase 0A Technical Proposal

**Project Dyson, Phase 0: Space Resource Processing (revised architecture, post-2026 re-assessment)**
**Item owner:** Governance & Legal. **Status:** Proposal for the configuration baseline; not yet adopted.
**Funding status:** 0A funded under D-01. The 0B increment is shown separately and is sized at KDP-0B.

---

## 0. Executive summary

bom-0-7 is the legal, governance, regulatory and coordination infrastructure that makes the rest of Phase 0 legally executable. It covers:

- the entities that hold contracts, licences and liability;
- the authority that decides gates;
- the filings that make a spacecraft lawful to launch and operate;
- the independent review that keeps the programme honest.

It has no orbital mass, no orbital power and no propellant. Its failure mode is not cost overrun. Its failure mode is that a correctly built pathfinder sits on the ground because nobody holds an authorization, a frequency assignment or an export classification.

**My central recommendations**

| # | Recommendation | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **Two legal entities**: a member-governed Association (owner) and a separately accountable Operator (licence holder). A third entity only if the export study demands it. | Panel consensus. Separation limits tort and regulatory exposure of the owner. |
| R2 | **Select the Operator's licensing state by a must/want screen within 12 months.** Luxembourg is the lead candidate, the US the alternate. | Authorization lead times put this decision on the Phase 0A critical path (§7). |
| R3 | **Cost as a run-rate plus one-time costs, bounded to the 0A period. Do not use a 10-year total.** | D-01 funds 0A only. A 10-year figure pre-commits 0B organizational spend. |
| R4 | **0A cost: $64M central over a 7-year 0A** (plausible $40–100M; scenario corners $30–130M). This excludes programme contingency, which sits in bom-0-17. | §9 bottom-up estimate. |
| R5 | **0B increment: $34M central** (plausible $20–55M), authorized only at KDP-0B. | §9. |
| R6 | **No flight insurance premiums in bom-0-7.** bom-0-7 administers insurance and holds the requirement. Premiums travel with the flight item (bom-0-12, bom-0-4, bom-0-8). | Avoids scope conflation, which was the largest driver of round-2 spread. |
| R7 | **Liquidity reserve ($8–20M) and a wind-down/safe-disposal escrow ($3–10M for 0A) are financing lines, not expenditure.** | Panel consensus on treatment. My own sizing. |
| R8 | **bom-0-7 owns the licence gate outright and the contract instrument for the demand gate.** | D-02. |
| R9 | **bom-0-7 owns command-authority policy and root-key custody for T26.** The comms service itself stays in bom-0-9 and bom-0-10. | T26 is architecture-changing. Authority and spectrum must not be locked to one architecture. |
| R10 | **Rate P0-F13 "major (schedule) / minor (cost)"** and track it on the critical path, not the cost register. | §7 critical-path analysis. |

**Where I depart from the round-2 envelope ($100–350M)**

My full-Phase-0 central estimate of about $98M sits at the bottom of that range, and my funded 0A commitment is about $64M. The gap comes from four things:

1. I exclude contingency, which would otherwise be double-counted with bom-0-17.
2. I exclude flight TPL premiums.
3. I refuse to pre-fund 0B-scale operations before KDP-0B.
4. My governance-archive cost is small, because engineering data belongs to bom-0-9 and PM/SE.

---

## 1. Design philosophy

1. **Authority before hardware.** Every flight item eventually needs an authorizing state, a registry entry, a frequency assignment, an export classification and a planetary-protection determination. These have fixed external lead times that money cannot compress. bom-0-7 is therefore scheduled backwards from the first pathfinder launch.

2. **Stringency follows reversibility (D-02).** The scale of approval depends on whether the decision can be undone:

   | Decision type | Examples | Approval |
   |---|---|---|
   | Reversible | Office location, tooling, advisory panel design | Officer level |
   | Hard to reverse | Licensing state, open licence choice, operator charter | Board, with legal opinion |
   | One-way | KDP-0B industrial commitment, any trajectory bringing >100 t toward Earth's vicinity | Both boards, independent review concurrence, public disclosure of any override |

3. **Separate owning from operating.** The Association decides what and whether. The Operator decides how, holds the licence and carries operational liability. A regulator must be able to identify one accountable operator. An owner that directs operations day-to-day risks being treated as the de facto operator.

4. **Open by default, closed by necessity, classified before release.** Designs are open (CERN OHL v2, CC BY-SA). Export-controlled data goes in a controlled annex. Command-authentication material is never published. Open design does not mean open keys.

5. **Govern what you can measure.** Every deliberation gets a disposition. Every gate has written pass criteria. Every number in the baseline has an owner, a basis and a falsifier.

6. **Small, professional core.** The organization runs on a core of roughly 16 FTE, with outside counsel used surgically. Volunteer contributors feed the engineering commons but do not hold licence-critical roles.

---

## 2. Scope definition (WBS dictionary entry)

### 2.1 In scope

| Code | Function | Notes |

| 7.1 | Legal entities and corporate governance | Formation, charters, boards, intercompany agreements, tax status, audit |

| 7.9 | Independent Cost Review (ICR) | Carried over from rq-0-28 |

### 2.2 Explicitly out of scope (with the owning item)

| ALARP debris analysis and the interim design-ceiling number | bom-0-15 (bom-0-7 carries it to the regulator) |

**Disagreement flagged (OQ-1).** The round-2 reconciliation proposed a PM/SE/MA line (D3, $1.5–3.5B). That line does not appear in the bom-0-1 to bom-0-17 list, and none of the listed items obviously contains it. It must not drift into bom-0-7: governance is not execution, and the panel was unanimous on that. Either create the line, or the WBS dictionary must show it embedded in each hardware item. This is the single largest unowned scope risk I can see in the Phase 0 BOM, and bom-0-7 should raise it at the first CCB.

---

## 3. Physical and resource specifications

bom-0-7 has no orbital hardware. Its resource envelope is:

| Parameter | Value | Range | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orbital mass | 0 t | 0 | Panel consensus, high confidence |
| Orbital power | 0 MW | 0 | Panel consensus |
| EP propellant | 0 t/yr | 0 | Panel consensus |
| Terrestrial power | 0.02 MW | 0.01–0.05 | 2 small offices (5–10 kW), 3 key-custody/HSM sites (≤1 kW each), archive nodes (1–3 kW). Mostly remote workforce. Not drawn from bom-0-5. |
| Staff, 0A steady state | 16 FTE | 14–20 | §8 |
| Staff, 0A ramp (years 1–2) | 10 FTE | 8–12 | §8 |
| Staff, 0B increment | +6 FTE | +4–8 | §8 |
| Legal entities | 2 | 2–3 | §4 |

| Root-key custody sites | 3 | 3 | 3-of-5 quorum, ≥2 jurisdictions (§6) |
| Governance archive ingest | 1 TB/yr | 0.5–3 | Board, legal, regulatory and disposition records |
| Released-baseline escrow ingest | 10 TB/yr | 5–20 | Released configuration baselines only. Not raw telemetry. |
| Archive copies | 3, independently administered | 3 | Panel consensus |
| Archive restore test | Annual full restore; quarterly sample restore | — | Annual is the panel figure. I add quarterly samples, because restore failures are usually found late. |

**Archive sizing check.** Over a 7-year 0A, about 77 TB of logical data is held in 3 copies, roughly 230 TB raw. At cloud-archive or tape costs of about $1–5/TB-month, storage is $0.05–0.15M/yr even at the end of 0A. Labour and testing dominate. I therefore disagree with Gemini's $10M archive line: the governance archive costs under $3M across all of 0A, labour included.

---

## 4. System architecture: entities and governance

### 4.1 Entity structure

```

  (Swiss Verein     │  Board: 7 (5–9), 3-yr staggered, max 2 terms│
   provisional;     │  Reserved matters only:                     │
   co-location      │   • charter & mission  • KDP-0B approval    │
   with Operator    │   • Operator board appointments (minority)  │
   state preferred  │   • budget envelope   • open-licence policy │

                           │ (reserved matters list)    │ agreement
                    ┌──────▼────────────────────────────▼─────────┐
  ENTITY B          │        OPERATOR (licence holder)             │
  (Luxembourg lead; │  Board: 5 — 2 Association-nominated,        │
   US alternate;    │         3 independent (space/legal/finance) │
   selected by J-   │  Holds: mission authorizations, registry    │
   gate, §7)        │   entries, ITU assignments (via admin),     │
                    │   prime/sub contracts, insurance, export    │
                    │   licences, root command authority          │
                    │  Committees: Safety (hosts ISA), Audit/Risk │
                    └──────┬───────────────┬────────────────┬─────┘
                           │               │                │
                 ┌─────────▼───┐   ┌───────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼────────┐
                 │ Programme   │   │ Independent  │  │ General       │
                 │ Director    │   │ Safety Auth. │  │ Counsel /     │
                 │ (PM/SE/MA — │   │ (reports to  │  │ Regulatory    │

                 └─────────────┘   └──────────────┘
```

**Why the Operator has an independent-majority board.** A regulator applying "authorization and continuing supervision" (Outer Space Treaty Art. VI) needs to see that the licensee itself controls operations. If the Association's nominees held a majority and the Association directed operations, the owner could be treated as the operator. That would erode the separation that justifies two entities. Under this design the Association controls *whether* through its reserved matters. It does not control *how*.

**Disagreement with Gemini's Option 2 detail.** In Gemini's Option 2 the Verein "sorts trustees." I would not give a sortition body any appointment power over the licence holder in Phase 0. The evidence base for sortition in asset-holding or safety-critical governance is low; Claude and GPT are right on this, and Gemini's "high, literature" label should be downgraded. In Phase 0, sortition is used only for an **advisory panel** of 15–25 members on values questions: openness versus export restriction, and the distribution of resource benefits. That panel has a published-response obligation, not a veto.

**Charter Trust.** This is a Phase 0 design study only: $0.3–1.0M, including a red-team takeover exercise and funding-control simulations. The establishment decision is made at a milestone no earlier than KDP-0B.

### 4.2 Operator jurisdiction selection (decision J, due month 12)

Must-criteria are pass/fail. Weighting cannot rescue an option that fails one.

| Must-criterion | Test |
|---|---|
| M1 | A national regime under which a private deep-space resource mission can be authorized and supervised |
| M2 | The state's ITU administration will file and maintain space research service networks for the operator |
| M3 | A non-profit-owned operator is eligible to hold the authorization |
| M4 | Export-control regime compatible with open publication of non-controlled design data |
| M5 | State is party to the OST, Liability and Registration Conventions |

Want-criteria (weights illustrative, not measured utilities):

| Want-criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Authorization clarity and lead time | 0.25 |
| Liability and insurance regime (required limits, state indemnity) | 0.20 |
| Launch and industrial access | 0.20 |
| Neutrality and political durability | 0.15 |
| Tax and charitable treatment of intra-group flows | 0.10 |
| Cost of presence | 0.10 |

**Candidates and my prior** (to be overturned by counsel opinions; every legal statement here needs counsel verification):

- **Luxembourg (lead).** It has a dedicated space-resources law (2017) and a space-activities authorization law (2020) (*verify both*). It has an established agency and administration, and is neutral within Europe. Weakness: launch access is entirely third-party.
- **United States (alternate).** CSLCA 2015 recognizes resource rights for US citizens (51 U.S.C. ch. 513, *verify*), and launch and industrial access is strong. Weakness: there is no settled mission-authorization path for novel in-space activities (*verify current status*). ITAR/EAR exposure also hits a programme whose charter mandates open publication.
- **Japan.** It has a 2021 space-resources act (*verify*) and is a credible alternate. Weaknesses: language and cost of presence, and less familiarity with non-profit operators.
- **Switzerland as Operator state.** I do not recommend it as the baseline. Its status should be verified, but Claude reports no comprehensive space act in force. The panel's caution not to assert Swiss law "from stale text" applies to the Association location as well.

**Decision rule.** Run M1–M5 with written counsel opinions in each of 3–4 states ($0.5–1.5M). Hold one pre-application meeting with each surviving regulator. Score the survivors. Tie-break: co-locate the Association with the Operator. One regulator and one tax authority beats Swiss neutrality if the scores are close.

### 4.3 Board and term parameters

| Body | Size | Term | Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Association Board | 7 (5–9) | 3 yr staggered (2-2-3) | 2 consecutive terms | Thirds rotate, so no wholesale capture in one election |
| Operator Board | 5 | 3 yr staggered | 3 terms for independents | Majority independent. Licence-relevant fitness test. |
| Standing Review Board (SRB) | 5–7 external, part-time | Per-gate engagement | — | Supports ISA and ICR at KDPs |
| Advisory sortition panel | 15–25 | 18 months | 1 | Stipended. Published-response obligation. |
| Leadership overlap on executive succession | 6 months | 3–12 | — | Mandatory handover for General Counsel, ISA head and Secretary-General |

**Funding caps.** These are disclosed targets: no single funder above 25% of 3-year trailing revenue. A time-limited exception of up to 24 months is allowed, with board resolution and public disclosure. Hard caps would make 0A unfundable in early years. Undisclosed concentration is the actual capture risk.

---

## 5. Subsystem specifications

### 5.1 Regulatory authorization and licensing (7.2)

**Deliverables**

- **Pathfinder (bom-0-12) mission authorization dossier.** Mission description, safety case, debris ALARP case, planetary-protection determination request, insurance evidence and registration data.
- **0B pre-authorization dossier**, prepared in late 0A. It feeds the licence gate.
- A regulator engagement log and a commitments register. Every promise made to a regulator becomes a tracked requirement in the baseline.

**Key regulatory insight from D-04 (SEL1 receiving node)**

0B tugs will deliver 150–300 t Fe-Ni payloads to Sun–Earth L1, about 1.5 × 10⁶ km from Earth. Two consequences follow:

1. **Earth-proximity hazard.** A 300 t iron mass is about a 4.2 m sphere (ρ ≈ 7,900 kg/m³). Iron bodies of this size survive atmospheric entry in part. An Earth-impact probability requirement per transfer and per fleet-year is therefore a licensing driver for 0B, not just a good-practice item.
   - The analysis belongs to bom-0-15 and mission design.
   - bom-0-7 owns negotiating the threshold with the licensing state, in line with D-03's ALARP-plus-interim-ceiling approach.
   - I recommend proposing the regulator be asked to accept a ceiling no looser than 10⁻⁶ per transfer for Earth-intersecting failure modes, with ALARP below that. This is a placeholder for the D-03 process, not a baseline number.
2. **Third-party liability is no longer negligible in 0B.** Damage on Earth's surface falls under absolute liability (Liability Convention Art. II). This contradicts the round-2 assumption that deep-space operations have "essentially no third parties." That holds for 0A NEA operations and the pathfinder cruise. It does not hold for 0B deliveries to SEL1. Claude's own reopening trigger ("if bom-0-4 brings material toward Earth") is met by D-04.

**Planetary protection**

- COSPAR policy is guidance implemented by the national authority. It is not a permit and is not "filed with COSPAR."
- The expected outcome is Category II for the NEA and Category V "unrestricted Earth return" logic for any Earth-approaching product. This must be a mission-specific determination.
- **Open point.** It is not established whether delivery to SEL1 without atmospheric entry is treated as "Earth return." bom-0-7 requests a formal determination at pre-application.

### 5.2 Spectrum and ITU (7.3)

- **Two ITU regimes.** The NEA site (at >2 × 10⁶ km) is deep space under the ITU definition (RR No. 1.177, *verify*). The SEL1 node (about 1.5 × 10⁶ km) is **not** deep space and uses near-Earth space research allocations. Phase 0 therefore needs filings in both regimes.

  | Location | Regime | Typical bands (indicative) |
  |---|---|---|
  | NEA site | Deep-space SRS | X: 7145–7190 MHz up / 8400–8450 MHz down. Ka: 34.2–34.7 GHz up / 31.8–32.3 GHz down. |
  | SEL1 node | Near-Earth SRS | S: 2025–2110 / 2200–2290 MHz. X: 8450–8500 MHz. Ka: 25.5–27 GHz down. |

- **Architecture-neutral filings (T26 linkage).** T26 is TRL 3 with AD² 4, flagged "architecture-change." The comms architecture may move away from DSN-style apertures, for example to commercial deep-space ground networks or optical. Filings must therefore cover X and Ka in both regimes, so that no architecture change forces a re-filing. Optical links are largely outside ITU coordination, but they need national coordination for ground laser safety.
- **Lead time.** Advance publication information is normally submitted no earlier than about 7 years and no later than about 2 years before bringing into use (*verify current RR provisions*). This sets the first critical-path milestone (§7).
- **Cost.** ITU cost-recovery fees run roughly CHF 10–100k per filing depending on complexity (*verify*), plus administration fees. $0.1–0.4M/yr is allowed.

### 5.3 Space-resources legal programme (7.4, from rq-0-14)

- Opinions on resource-rights recognition in the Operator state.
- Compatibility with the Artemis Accords and positions taken in the UN COPUOS working group on space resources (*verify current status*).
- Treatment of Fe-Ni product transferred to a Phase 1 entity, which may be in a different state.
- Benefit-sharing policy, as a values question for the Association and its advisory panel.
- **Budget: $2–6M one-time (central $3.5M) plus 1 FTE.**

**Note on rq-0-14 "25 kt/yr".** Its meaning is undefined. If it means hydrogen output, it implies 140–190 MW of electrolysis, which is incompatible with Phase 0. It also conflicts with the current 0.6–2.5 kt/yr product range and with the abandoned LOX/LH₂ line. bom-0-7 dispositions it as **SUPERSEDED** and records the reason in the register. It does not carry it forward as a legal scale assumption.

### 5.4 Export control and release classification (7.5)

A three-tier release model:

```
  ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Author/owner  │───▶│ Classification gate   │───▶│ Tier assignment  │
  │ submits item  │    │ (Export Control Off.) │    └───┬────┬────┬────┘
  └───────────────┘    │ SLA: 10 working days  │        │    │    │
                       │ standard; 30 days if  │        ▼    ▼    ▼
                       │ agency ruling needed  │     OPEN  CTRL  SEC
                       └───────────────────────┘
  OPEN : CERN-OHL-S v2 (designs), CC BY-SA 4.0 (docs), CC BY 4.0
         (interface standards), Apache-2.0 (software). Public repo.
  CTRL : Controlled annex. Named-person access under licence/TCP.
         Expected: EP thruster detail, some GNC, certain processing
         know-how (verify categories; ITAR USML XV / EAR 9x515
         candidates).
  SEC  : Command authentication, key material, vulnerability data.
         Never published. Need-to-know.
```

- **Initial full-baseline classification: $0.5–2.0M one-time**, including any formal jurisdiction or commodity-classification requests.
- **Release SLA metrics:** at least 90% of items within 10 working days. The publication-compliance target is 0 unclassified releases. Any breach triggers a root-cause review reported to the Operator Audit/Risk Committee.
- **Licence choice (my opinion).**
  - CERN OHL v2-S for project-originated hardware.
  - CC BY 4.0 rather than BY-SA for interface standards. Interfaces should be maximally adoptable, including by proprietary suppliers to Phase 1.
  - Apache-2.0 for software. OHL does not cover software well, and Apache's patent grant matters.
  - This narrows the panel's "CERN OHL v2 + CC" consensus. It does not contradict it.

### 5.5 IP policy for industrial partners (7.13, 0B-relevant)

- **Partner background IP**, such as proprietary process know-how, may remain proprietary. It must carry:
  - a perpetual, royalty-free licence-back to the Operator for programme use;
  - source or know-how escrow released if the partner exits.

## 7. Development roadmap and critical path

### 7.1 Why P0-F13 is "major (schedule)"

The external lead times, working backwards from a pathfinder launch at year L:

```
  ITU API / filings          ≥2 yr before bringing into use (verify)
  National authorization     12–24 months review (typical; verify per state)
  Pre-application dialogue    6–12 months before lodging
  Operator entity existence   needed before pre-application (licensee identity)
  Jurisdiction selection      needed before operator formation
  Counsel opinions            3–6 months
```

Critical chain: opinions (0.5 yr), then selection (0.25), then formation (0.5), then pre-application (0.75), then authorization review (1.5), with roughly a 1.0 yr margin to launch. That is **about 4.5 years of bom-0-7 lead before pathfinder launch**.

ITU filings run in parallel but must start by about L−3 years.

If the pathfinder (bom-0-12) is to fly about 5–6 years after 0A start, then **bom-0-7 is on the critical path from month 0**. This is the falsifiable basis for the severity label. The label becomes **minor (schedule)** if the approved pathfinder launch date is more than 7 years after 0A start. That is the same falsifier Claude proposed, and I adopt it.

**Cost of delay.** A one-year slip of Phase 0A idles hardware teams and holds programme cost. It plausibly costs $80–160M per year of slip against bom-0-7's roughly $8M/yr, so delay costs about 10–20× the function itself at central values. This ratio is a judgement, not a measurement.
